Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters Seascape: the state of our oceans Plastics UK plastic ‘waste colonialism’ found to be polluting Turkey’s farming heartland A Guardian investigation finds irrigation canals polluted with microplastics in Turkey, a major destination for UK waste ‘Nobody cares’: Turkish farmers bear the burden of UK’s plastic waste problem Seascape: the state of our oceans is supported by About this content Karen McVeigh and Ayça Aldatmaz in Adana Tue 4 Aug 2026 05.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 05.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google High levels of microplastics and other plastic contamination have been discovered in a waterway close to a major recycling hub in Turkey supplied with plastic waste by British companies. The polluted waterway, which floods into agricultural fields after heavy rain, feeds into a larger canal used for irrigating crops on the Çukurova plain, in the city of Adana, in the south of the country. It is one of the largest and most fertile agricultural basins in Turkey. The findings from a Guardian investigation reignite concerns over Britain’s continuing role in “waste colonialism” – a term used to describe the export of plastic waste by rich nations to poorer countries with less regulated waste management. The UK government pledged to reduce plastic pollution and eliminate harmful plastics during talks to reach a global plastics treaty , which collapsed last year, but it has not committed to a ban on exports. Treaty negotiations are expected to resume in 2027. Britain, one of the world’s largest exporters of plastic waste, exported 675,000 tonnes in 2025, its largest amount in eight years, of which 139,000 tonnes was shipped to Turkey . The EU’s plastic waste exports to Turkey that year rose 19% on the year before to more than 500,000 tonnes . Environmental campaigners in the UK and Turkey say that British and EU plastic waste exports are driving the operations responsible for the pollution, leaving the city’s poorer residents to pay the price. About 13% of UK plastic waste to Turkey was shipped to eight facilities within the recycling zone in Adana between May 2021 and July 2024, according to an analysis of import and export data carried out for the Guardian by an international NGO, the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA). Thirteen British companies sent 545 shipments, totalling 52,000 tonnes, of plastic waste to the hub during the three-year period. There is no suggestion that the companies exporting plastic waste are acting illegally. British exporters of plastic waste do, however, have a duty under various regulations to ensure that the plastic they export is recycled in an environmentally sound manner. View image in fullscreen A plastic waste recycling plant near Adana. Samples taken from a canal downstream from the recycling zone were 10 times higher than upstream sites. Photograph: Ayça Aldatmaz Sedat Gündoğdu, a Turkish marine biologist at Sabancı University’s Istanbul Policy Center, who conducted the microplastic sampling, has called for a ban on all plastic imports to Turkey. “The discharge of microplastic-laden wastewater into irrigation canals raises critical concerns about agricultural contamination and food safety,” he said. Plastic pollution from recycling centres that contaminates canals ultimately ends up in the Mediterranean Sea, he added, which “exacerbates marine plastic accumulation” and undermines efforts to protect the sea from contamination. Samples taken from the canal downstream from the recycling zone were 10 times higher than upstream sites, according to Gündoğdu’s research, published in Environment Monitoring and Assessment . He also found pellets, films and fragments “highly characteristic of [waste] recycling processing”, he said. He has called for mandatory installation of microplastic filtration at all facilities and independent monitoring of all wastewater discharges in agricultural zones. Amy Youngman, a legal specialist at the EIA, said that, by its continued reliance on exporting rather than investing in reduction or domestic recycling, the UK had failed to “keep pace with the EU” and had created a “structural imbalance”. “This results in pollution occurring overseas in ways that would not be tolerated within the UK itself and passes the devastating human health, economic and environmental harm to communities in Turkey,” she said. The findings added to an “expanding body of irrefutable evidence exposing waste colonialism in the UK’s waste-export system”, she said. We need to talk about plastic: five everyday items choking the planet Read more A Greenpeace investigation in 2021 found plastic waste from British supermarkets waste dumped and burned in Adana . The same year, the Turkish government announced a ban on certain waste, including polyethylene , which is used in 94% of UK plastic waste exports including yoghurt pots, salad bags and plastic film, but revoked the ban after pressure from the recycling industry . The EU has recently imposed strict controls on plastic waste exports . From November, exports other than to mostly rich OECD countries will be banned. Environmentalists fear this could lead to more exports to Turkey, an OECD country and already the main importer of EU waste. A spokesperson for the UK’s Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs said: “There are already strict controls in place on the export of waste set out in UK legislation. Businesses involved in the export of waste from the UK are required to ensure that the waste they ship is managed in an environmentally sound manner, and we have already taken action to further reduce our need to export plastic waste.” The Turkish government was approached for comment but did not respond. https://www.politico.eu/article/peter-ma.text: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s ruling Tisza party said on Saturday that it had nominated former Supreme Court President András Baka to become the country’s next president. Baka, who worked as a judge on the European Court of Human Rights before being elected to head the Supreme Court, was removed from his post by the Fidesz government in 2011 — a move the ECHR ruled was unlawful . “Throughout his career, Dr. András Baka has considered the principle of the separation of powers to be of paramount importance and has consistently stood up for the rule of law and judicial independence,” Tisza said in a Facebook post . Advertisement Advertisement He is “the strongest guarantee that the office of President of the Republic will regain its true dignity and its ability to unite the nation and serve as a counterbalance to the ruling majority,” it added. Parliament is set to vote on his candidacy next Tuesday. Tisza, which won a general election in the spring, enjoys a two-thirds majority in the chamber, making Baka’s election to the largely representative post a formality. The nomination comes after former President Tamás Sulyok signed a constitutional amendment that removed him from office last month, bowing to months of public pressure from Magyar. The new prime minister had called for Sulyok’s resignation following Tisza’s landslide election victory that ended Viktor Orbán’s 16-year rule. Magyar’s first choice for president, chess grandmaster Judit Polgár, declined the nomination, saying the job would be too stressful .

Photograph: David McHugh/Brighton Pictures West Sussex Three dead after family get into difficulty in water off Shoreham-by-Sea A man, woman and teenage girl have died, while a younger girl is in a critical condition, say Sussex police Nadeem Badshah Tue 18 Aug 2026 18.23 EDT First published on Tue 18 Aug 2026 16.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A couple and their teenage daughter have died after getting into difficulty in the sea off the West Sussex coast, police said on Tuesday. A man, a woman and a teenage girl died after the incident in Shoreham-by-Sea, the chief superintendent of Sussex police, James Collis, said. A younger girl from the same family was taken to hospital in a critical condition, Collis added. The next of kin have been informed. Collis said it is understood that all four got into difficulty in the water after going for a swim. He added: “Our thoughts are with the friends and family. I know this incident will have a profound effect on the community.” Emergency services were called at about 2.40pm to reports of four people in difficulty in the sea. All four were brought to shore. The coastguard is not searching for anyone else. A spokesperson for Air Ambulance Charity Kent Surrey Sussex said both of its helicopters and critical care team had been sent to the scene as part of the response, and Shoreham RNLI said its lifeboat had been called out at 3pm. Tom Rutland, the MP for Shoreham, offered his condolences. “My thoughts are with the family and friends of those who have lost their lives, and I know the whole community here in Shoreham will be hoping and praying for the recovery of the young girl receiving medical treatment in hospital,” he said. A local said the water was “incredibly rough” and the winds were “incredibly strong”, Sky News reported. Rutland thanked the emergency services, which he said “responded swiftly” and “worked tirelessly in exceptionally difficult circumstances”. Speaking at a press conference, Collis added: “At this point we believe all four entered the water from the land to swim and sadly got into difficulty. Our partners in His Majesty’s Coastguard have completed an extensive search of the water and we are not searching for anyone else. “I would like to thank the public for their patience and understanding during the emergency response. The A259 Brighton Road was blocked in both directions from New Road to Kingston Lane because of the incident. There have been a number of water-related deaths in recent months during the extreme heat. On Saturday, a 12-year-old boy drowned in the River Lea, near the Hackney Marshes, in north-east London. In April, a woman and her young child died after getting into difficulty in the water in west London. Both died at the scene in Elthorne Park, Ealing, the Metropolitan police said. Anyone with information or with video footage relating to the incident in Shoreham-by-Sea should contact Sussex police. https://nypost.com/2026/09/18/world-news.text: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk issued a chilling warning to NATO allies Thursday: Russian President Vladimir Putin is plotting a hybrid attack on European nations backing Ukraine — with Poland and other close neighbors directly in the crosshairs. Tusk warned the impending attacks will be staged as “hybrid” or fake “accidents” designed to paralyze Western response and shatter NATO’s resolve. “There is a real risk that drones or other types of projectiles will enter the territory of one or several countries on the eastern flank and even cause destruction,” he said in a speech to the Polish parliament. 6 Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk at the Prime Minister’s Office in Warsaw, Poland on Thursday. RADEK PIETRUSZKA/EPA/Shutterstock “The official narrative will be that it’s an accident and there is no reason for NATO to think about a response,” he added. Under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, an armed attack against one member state is considered an attack against all — the core principle meant to deter aggression against alliance members. The “accident” narrative is meant to circumvent that promise among NATO members. Tusk raised the alarm over Russia’s deadly new tactics, pointing out their reliance on high-speed, jet-powered drones that fly higher and faster — making them nearly impossible for air defenses to intercept before impact. Explore More Race against time to save crew after colossal, rarely seen deep sea beasts smash up yacht in Pacific Saudi Arabia and Jordan denied flydubai flight clearance to land despite a terrifying mayday call Accused plane hijacker is religious extremist who refused to shake women’s hands He has been warning for months that Russia might be preparing a more serious hybrid attack against a NATO member state. The Polish leader’s dire predictions have grown increasingly precise as high-level intelligence pours in from NATO, Kyiv and the CIA. Moscow’s war machine is currently focused on strangling critical supply lines between Ukraine and its allies, unleashing strikes near the Polish and Moldovan borders. Tusk emphasized that Russia has zero interest in peace talks without the “total capitulation of Ukraine.” 6 Poland shot down drones that entered its airspace during a widespread Russian attack in western Ukraine, Wednesday. Obtained by NYPost “They are convinced the winter will be tragically critical for Ukraine,” Tusk said. While Poland has rushed to bolster Ukraine’s battered power grid, Tusk cautioned that crippling key border hubs would paralyze Warsaw’s ability to assist its neighbor through the winter. “Russia’s goal is to destroy as much as possible the economy and logistics of Ukraine,” he said, revealing intel that points to an upcoming barrage of “very high frequency and intensity” across six key Ukrainian cities. In defiance of Moscow, Tusk announced he would travel to Kyiv overnight into Friday — coming just days after European leaders narrowly dodged a Russian drone strike near the border. 6 Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that he was in constant contact with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte following the incident. Obtained by NYPost Typically, high-level government officials keep their travel plans to Ukraine secret for security reasons. In Kyiv, Tusk will convene with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on how to defend against Russia’s new drone hardware and discuss more sanctions against Russia with Slovakian officials. President Trump appears keen to help out. On Thursday, he said on Truth Social that “major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army Base in Poland” after an American delegation visited the country last week to survey possible locations. “If this happens, the location will be announced very soon,” Trump wrote. 6 Polish National Territorial Defense Forces are at the crash site of a Russian drone in the village of Wohyn, eastern Poland, Wednesday, Sept. 10, 2025. WOJTEK JARGILO/EPA/Shutterstock “This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance.” Poland has sought to host a permanent American military base for guaranteed security against a potential Russian threat. The Eastern European country is a top spender in NATO relative to the size of its economy, allocating a record 4.8% of its GDP to defense in 2026, according to National Defense Magazine . Poland’s massive defense push and major US arms deals have directed the Trump administration toward authorizing a permanent American footprint in the country, even as the Pentagon scales back forces elsewhere in Europe. In May, the US unexpectedly withdrew troops from the total of around 10,000 stationed in Poland, causing confusion among European allies and creating anxiety in Warsaw. 6 A Russian-made Gerbera drone recovered by the Moldovan police is exposed on the stairs at the entrance of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Moldova in Chisinau, Wednesday. AFP via Getty Images Officials in Poland and the US soon clarified that the withdrawal is temporary and poses no risk to Polish national security. Russia bombarded Kyiv and other cities with missiles and drones overnight from Wednesday into Thursday, and neighboring NATO member Poland scrambled jets ‌after a Russian daytime attack in western Ukraine, officials said on Thursday. Over 20 people were injured in the overnight strikes, Ukrainian officials said. The attacks follow the passage of a sweeping sanctions bill in the House of Representatives Wednesday that tightened economic pressure on Russia and fulfilled a last wish of Sen. Lindsey Graham, two months after his death. The “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026” was named in honor of the South Carolina senator who died at age 71 following a trip to Ukraine where he championed the legislation. It passed the Senate last month. President Trump is expected to sign the act into law. The legislation targets Russia and Iran — hitting those that support the Kremlin’s war on Ukraine and curbing funding for Iranian energy and weapons programs. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Monday that Russian drone strikes on Sunday near the Ukraine-Poland border — one of which hit a train shortly after senior visiting officials had passed through the same station — would drive the military alliance to increase its support for Kyiv, labeling the bombardments as a sign of Moscow’s growing desperation. 6 A screen grab taken from video footage released by the TVN channel shows a suspected Russian military drone recovered from the Baltic Sea off Poland’s coast near the village of Rusinowo, Monday. AFPTV/TVN/AFP via Getty Images The strikes “close to NATO territory” show Putin’s “desperation and also his desire to sow fear and terror,” Rutte said at NATO’s political headquarters in Brussels. “Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine,” he exclaimed. “He thinks that he can stop us from supporting Ukraine and that he can undermine our unity. He is wrong,” the NATO chief said of Putin. Photograph: Matthew Dae Smith/AP View image in fullscreen Larry Nassar in court in Charlotte, Michigan, in February 2018. Photograph: Matthew Dae Smith/AP Michigan Michigan state police rule out claim that Larry Nassar was removed from sex offender registry Eaton county prosecuting attorney’s office had said court ruling forced removal of Nassar’s name – but he wasn’t on list because he was imprisoned out of state Guardian staff Sat 3 Oct 2026 10.07 EDT First published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 17.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Michigan has removed more than 20,000 entries from its sex offender registry, but convicted serial abuser Larry Nassar is not one of them – the former Michigan State University and USA Gymnastics doctor was not in that system, as a local prosecutor’s office claimed, because he was serving an out-of-state federal prison sentence, according to state police. On 9 September, the Michigan supreme court ruled that the state’s Sex Offender Registration Act (Sora) cannot be applied retroactively to cases involving offenses committed before the law’s relevant date. Michigan’s state police, as a result, removed more than 20,000 people whose offenses occurred before 1 July 2011 from the agency’s online sex offender database. One of the agencies to prosecute Nassar, the Eaton county prosecuting attorney’s office, asserted that he was among those removed from the Michigan state police sex offender registry. The office – helmed by Republican Michigan state attorney general candidate Doug Lloyd – even shared a screenshot showing a search for his name returning zero results. The office also published a statement that read: “The Michigan supreme court’s decision to eliminate Sora requirements for these offenders is deeply concerning.” The statement was widely reported on in the news media, and it added: “Our community, along with the victims of these crimes, expected the registry to provide a measure of protection and awareness – assurances that have now been removed by the court’s ruling.” But on Friday, Michigan state police released their own statement saying: “Information suggesting that convicted sex offender Nassar was removed from the sex offender registry by the Michigan state police because of the Smith decision is incorrect.” US Bureau of Prisons records show Nassar has been imprisoned at Pennsylvania’s Lewisburg federal correctional institute – and “offenders not currently domiciled, temporarily residing, working, incarcerated or going to school in Michigan do not have the duty to register in Michigan under [Sora], and would not be visible on Michigan’s public sex offender registry”, the state police statement said. “Should the offender later domicile (including being incarcerated), temporarily reside, work or go to school in Michigan, they would be expected to register and be placed on Michigan’s public [sex offender registry] if still required under Sora at that time.” The Eaton county prosecuting attorney’s office on Friday issued a statement, too, saying : “We must correct our earlier social media post about removal of convicted sex offenders from the Michigan sex offender registry … We never contemplated that one of the most notorious sex offenders in the history of the state would not have been registered despite the law requiring otherwise.” The office noted that offenses for which Nassar was convicted in Eaton county and neighboring Ingham county had 2009 and 1998 dates associated with them, which “fall within the time frame [of] the recent supreme court order”. At the time he was sentenced for those offenses in 2018, he was incarcerated in Michigan and would have been required to be registered as a sex offender in the state until being transferred into federal custody out of state, according to the Eaton prosecuting attorney’s office’s statement. “We apologize for the confusion,” the office’s statement said. But the statement also said: “As prosecutors, we have a responsibility to provide information to victims and survivors of sexual assault.” Michigan lawmakers do not have the authority to reverse the state supreme court’s decision. However, the legislature could pass new legislation that would place the affected offenders back in the database. Nassar was sentenced in 2018 to as many as 175 years in state and federal prison after being convicted of sexually abusing women and girls for decades while working at Michigan State University and serving as a doctor for Team USA Gymnastics. As of Friday, Nassar’s projected earliest release date for his federal prison sentence was in 2068, when he would be 104. More than 150 women and girls have accused Nassar of assault. His accusers include Olympic gold medal-winning gymnasts Aly Raisman, Simone Biles, McKayla Maroney and Gabby Douglas. Nassar pleaded guilty in November 2017 to multiple counts of first-degree criminal sexual conduct. He survived being stabbed multiple times in July 2023 while imprisoned. During his sentencing hearing, his accusers delivered impact statements describing the shame and trauma they said they experienced because of Nassar. Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). https://www.azernews.az/region/264663.ht.text: Slovakia to receive extra €105 million from EU over military supplies to Ukraine 29 September 2026 14:26 (UTC+04:00) Ulviyya Poladova Read more The European Union (EU) will provide Slovakia with an additional €105 million in compensation for military equipment supplied to Ukraine. Slovakia’s Ministry of Defence Director General for Defence Policy Robert Bestro said the funds would be allocated from the European Peace Facility and added to previously provided compensation. It was previously reported that Slovakia, under the former government, supplied Ukraine with MiG-29 fighter jets and S-300 air defence systems. The current government has abandoned the policy of providing military aid from state resources but allows Slovak companies to make commercial supplies to Ukraine. The current Slovak government has ended the practice of donating weapons and ammunition to Ukraine. However, Slovak companies are permitted to supply weapons to Ukraine on a commercial basis. At the beginning of September, the Slovak government approved a proposal to join the Convention establishing an International Claims Commission for Ukraine. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, A man offers residents in Kherson, Ukraine, the use of his Starlink internet after a Russian strike By Tiffany Wertheimer Published 25 October 2026, 00:00 BST Updated 4 hours ago Ukraine is in desperate need of a new satellite internet service, but a fast and reliable alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink network simply doesn't exist - yet. Last week's sudden slowdown of the service in Ukraine, which affected Kyiv's ability to defend itself from Russian attacks, has shown how vulnerable the country can be, and sharply increased Europe's urgency to have its own military-grade satellite network. That vulnerability was highlighted by Musk himself on Saturday, when he accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by using it for "drone strikes to kill people". Saying that loophole was closed last week, he wrote on X , external : "Violation of those terms will result in end of service." He added: "Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately". How Starlink works on the battlefield Published 15 October There are a few alternatives, but they are all lagging behind Starlink, which is the world's largest satellite constellation. France's Eutelsat, with its OneWeb internet service, is the main alternative - but it only has about 600 active satellites, compared with Starlink's 10,000-plus. The EU is working on a new network to rival Starlink, IrisÂ², however it won't be up and running until 2029. For Ukraine's troops on the ground, several of whom spoke anonymously to the BBC, reliable connectivity is the difference between life and death. "God forbid they shut it off completely, it would be an absolute catastrophe," said one. "I don't give a damn how much an alternative costs when our lives are on the line." For now, Ukraine's best bet is to join Govsatcom, the EU's satellite sharing network - but it cannot be used for military warfare like controlling drones. Figure caption, Watch: Who controls Ukraine's access to Starlink? Why does Starlink dominate in Ukraine? Starlink and its military-grade service, Starshield, are both owned by Musk's SpaceX company and have dominated the global satellite market for years. Ukraine relies on Starlink for communications on the battlefield and Starshield, which is controlled by the US government, for military purposes like drone warfare. The network is able to provide fast, real-time connectivity, which is crucial for defence and intercepting Russian attacks. "You can't employ drone warfare without this kind of high-speed internet connection," said Vincent Tourret, a researcher at the French Institute of International Relations. Last week's slowdown, which has only just been restored , highlighted the risks of relying on a US provider at a time when tensions between Kyiv and Washington continue to deteriorate. "Ukraine's defence cannot depend on Trump's or Musk's whims," French MEP, Christophe Grudler, tweeted. Who authorised the Starlink restrictions is still not clear, with a confusing blame-game ongoing between the Pentagon, Donald Trump and Musk. While Starlink has been one of Ukraine's greatest assets in this conflict, the "flipside of that dependence" has been exposed, explained Kari Bingen, director of the Aerospace Security Project at CSIS. "This is a critical military capability that Ukraine relies on, but doesn't control." Image source, Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/ Getty Images Image caption, Ukrainian soldiers set up a Starlink terminal on the battlefield Starlink is not the only satellite network Ukraine can access, so if it goes down there are other options - but experts say they aren't as fast, and troops the BBC spoke to agree. Starlink "gives us the upper hand when it comes to passing commands - even one or two seconds are critical when we can transfer data and orders faster, and you can really feel that advantage on the battlefield", a soldier said. The terminals used to connect to the satellites are also an important factor. Starlink's are relatively small and lightweight, so they can be fixed to any kind of vehicle or drone. Eutelsat's terminals "are slightly larger, so they can be fitted on the roof of a car, or on tanks, but they can't necessarily sit on small drones", said Eva Berneke, former CEO of the French satellite company. They are also about five times more expensive, she added. What can the EU offer right now? Rhetoric from the White House - like Trump's scathing criticism of Nato and his threats against Greenland - have given the EU "some pretty brutal alarm bells", Berneke told the BBC. She had only been at Eutelsat for a month when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and said she noticed a marked change in urgency from European authorities, as they looked to her company to help plug holes left by Starlink if it could not be relied upon. Comments from Musk have further heightened the need for an alternative: "Be quiet, small man... there is no substitute for Starlink," he tweeted , external at Poland's foreign minister last year, when the politician said he would "look for other suppliers" if SpaceX was unreliable. Europe has realised its security depends on space, and it must "strengthen its satellite capacities, urgently", a spokesperson for the European Commission told the BBC. Right now, it has Govsatcom, a network that was set up in January to share existing satellites between EU member states. Ukraine is not a full-fledged member (although it is trying to become one), but the Commission is in talks with Kyiv to join Govsatcom. But even if Ukraine could connect tomorrow, the network could not be used for warfare operations like piloting drones, which Starshield is used for. That could change by the start of next year, however, when the European Commission hopes commercial companies, like Eutelsat's OneWeb, will join the programme. This will give Ukraine some - but not all - of its military network needs. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, French President Emmanuel Macron, with a Eutelsat terminal, at the International Paris Air Show last year Eva Berneke told the BBC she is confident the company will be able to "support quite a lot of Ukraine's key military needs". But meeting its communications needs is another thing because, as is the case with most countries, they are varied and massive. Eutelsat could not comment on Govsatcom, but told the BBC that "as the only European operator of a fully operational [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we are committed to providing resilient connectivity to the businesses, governments and communities we serve". No timeline has been given for when Ukraine will be able to join the Govsatcom network. When it does it will likely be as a reliable back-up to Starlink and Starshield. But that's better than nothing, Vincent Tourret said. "If Starlink is shut down, it's good to have another way to stay connected, but it won't be enough for strikes or interceptions, at this stage." IrisÂ² - The EU's future network Govsatcom is seen as a short-term safety net, until the stronger and more secure network, IrisÂ² , external is up and running in 2029. The ambitious project (pronounced Iris squared ) is Europe's answer to Starlink and Starshield. It will be a defence-first programme, the European Commission says, with a focus on governments, military and emergency services. Ukraine has been guaranteed access to it from day one. Part of the EU's space programme, the European satellite companies Eutelsat, SES and Hispasat are leading the project in a consortium called SpaceRISE. It will still have far fewer satellites than Starlink, with 348 across low and medium earth orbit - but that shouldn't be seen as a negative, said Kari Bingen. "Think about a flash light beaming down - those satellites will be able to cover a greater amount of the Earth, so you need fewer of them," she explained. "They're all trade offs - I would not take it as a negative, that IrisÂ² is planning for less satellites." Tourret was more sceptical: "It's no gamechanger and no great saviour, I'm afraid". Image source, Paul Hennessy/ Getty Images Image caption, A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, carrying 56 Starlink satellites, takes off from Cape Canaveral in March A highly produced video on the EU Space Policy's website declares: "With IrisÂ², Europe will no longer depend on others for satellite connectivity." So does that mean Ukraine could switch off Starlink? No - that wouldn't be a good idea. "Users need to think about communications resilience," Bingen said. "So if something happens to one system, you have other ways to maintain connectivity." It's similar to how mobile phones work, explained Eva Berneke: "If you don't have 5G, you go back to 4G. And if you don't have 4G, you might use 3G, so you have multiple networks for resilience. It's the same idea in warfare." But while a phone might not load pictures as quickly on 3G, for a drone operator, it can be deadly: "That is not a nice situation to have to be in when you're fighting a war." IrisÂ² is not the only option. This week, Finnish companies Nokia and ICEYE , external announced they would look at developing satellite communications for Ukraine's military defences. And a joint venture between European satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales, called Project Bromo, is hoped to be another competitor against SpaceX, but it is still in the very early phases. Space projects take a long time, Berneke said, and need " a lot of money". Designing the programme, making the satellites, launching them and then having enough of them in orbit for full coverage takes many years. "Even if you gave me â¬8bn right now, I don't think I could have anything up there before 2032-2033," she explained. Why Space is the new defence frontier Military work in Space is nothing new, and has been happening since the dawn of the space age in the 1950s. But the conflict in Ukraine has shown how integral it is to modern warfare. "Communication is so important, and terrestrial communication platforms, whether it's 5G or fibre, can be attacked on the ground," Berneke said. "It is a lot harder to shoot down an entire satellite network. That's not something any military can do right now." While we look to the skies, however, most of the world's communications are travelling via undersea cables - about 99% in fact. But these are vulnerable to attack - this week the UK government outlined new measures to protect its cables, after an increase in suspicious activity by Russian vessels. "In a crisis or conflict, there are serious concerns that undersea cables will be cut... so if that happens it's good to have satellite communication as a backup," Kari Bingen said.
